Chapter 3

Instructions from Traffic Controllers

When an authorised person directs traffic — who may give instructions, which signals you must recognise, and how those instructions interact with traffic lights, signs and the general traffic rules.

  • Obligations of Road Users
  • Precedence Rules

Chapter 3 explains the legally binding instructions that can be given by authorised persons and traffic controllers. Under Article 84 of the RVV 1990, a valid instruction takes precedence over traffic signs and traffic rules.

The rest of the precedence system is more specific than a simple four-level ladder: traffic lights take precedence over signs that regulate priority, while traffic signs take precedence over incompatible general traffic rules. This chapter shows how to apply those rules correctly.

§ 1 — Obligations of Road Users

Who may give legally binding traffic instructions, how those instructions are given, and how road users must respond.

Who May Give Binding Traffic Instructions? Article 82 RVV

Article 82 of the RVV 1990 requires road users to follow verbal or gestured instructions given by specific authorised persons who are identifiable as such. These include:

  • Authorised officials identifiable as such, including police officers when acting within their traffic-control powers.
  • Personnel of the Royal Marechaussee (Koninklijke Marechaussee), insofar as they are not already included among the authorised officials above.
  • Authorised traffic controllers (verkeersregelaars) who are identifiable as such.
  • Trainees during specified practical lessons or examinations, but only under the conditions laid down in Article 82 and while wearing the prescribed traffic-controller clothing.

Not everyone directing traffic has the same legal status or powers. Professional traffic controllers, transport escorts and event traffic controllers are appointed under different rules. School traffic wardens (verkeersbrigadiers) are a separate category; drivers must obey their official F10 stop signal.

Obligation to Follow Instructions All road users

Road users must follow a lawful instruction that is directed at them by an authorised and identifiable person. Under Article 84 RVV, such an instruction takes precedence over traffic signs and traffic rules when there is a conflict.

Make sure the instruction actually applies to you. A person who is merely present at the roadside, or a gesture that is not directed at your traffic stream, does not automatically replace the normal traffic-control system.

Instructions Can Override Red Lights Yes, really

A clear instruction from an authorised person can require you to proceed even though the traffic light is red, or to stop even though it is green. Article 84 gives instructions precedence over traffic signs and traffic rules.

The same principle can apply when an instruction conflicts with a turn restriction, a priority sign or another ordinary traffic rule. Follow the valid instruction that is directed at you, while continuing to avoid unnecessary danger.

The mere presence of a traffic controller does not switch off every traffic light or sign. What takes precedence is the instruction actually given to you or to your traffic stream.
Official Gesture Signals RVV Appendix

The Appendix to the RVV 1990 contains standard gesture signals that authorised persons use as far as possible. Learn the official stop and speed-reduction signals rather than relying on informal guesses about body position.

General stop signal
The official Appendix includes a general stop signal. Traffic to which the signal is directed must stop.
Stop — traffic approaching from the front
Traffic approaching the authorised person from the front must stop.
Stop — traffic approaching from behind
Traffic approaching the authorised person from behind must stop.
Stop — traffic from front and behind
Traffic approaching from both the front and the rear must stop.
Stop — traffic approaching from the right
Traffic approaching from the authorised person's right-hand side must stop.
Stop free-moving lanes / clear the junction
Traffic in the free-moving lanes must stop. Traffic in the other lanes may proceed with caution, and the junction must be cleared.
Reduce speed
This official gesture instructs approaching traffic to reduce speed.
Traffic warden — sign F10
Drivers must stop for the official F10 stop signal given by an authorised traffic warden (verkeersbrigadier).
Use the Official Signal, Not a Shortcut

The RVV Appendix defines several different stop signals. Do not reduce them to a single rule such as “front and back stop, sides go.” On the exam, identify the specific official gesture shown and apply its stated meaning.

Other Binding Stop Instructions Articles 82a & 83

The RVV also recognises certain stop instructions that are not ordinary hand gestures. Road users must obey qualifying illuminated instructions on authorised service vehicles. They must also stop for a red light or an illuminated STOP / STOP POLICE transparency shown from an authorised police vehicle or Rijkswaterstaat road-inspector vehicle.

Road users must also stop when the accompanying official of a rail vehicle gives the legally prescribed stop signal, red flag or red light.

Responding Safely to Instructions Practical guidance

When an authorised person gives you an instruction, respond promptly but safely. Avoid unnecessary sudden braking or swerving. If the instruction is unclear, reduce speed and seek clarification rather than guessing.

Do not ignore a clear instruction merely because a traffic light or sign appears to say something different. At the same time, remain responsible for avoiding unnecessary danger while carrying out the instruction.

Traffic Controllers at Roadworks Common scenario

Traffic controllers are frequently deployed at roadworks where normal traffic flow is disrupted. They manage alternating one-way sections, guide traffic around equipment, and respond to changing conditions in real time. At a roadworks site, their instructions may change rapidly — stay alert and watch the controller continuously, not just at the moment you first see them.

Traffic Controllers at Events Events & gatherings

At events, authorised event traffic controllers may be deployed to manage traffic around the site. They are appointed under specific rules and operate within the scope of that appointment; event traffic controllers work under police supervision. When an authorised and identifiable event traffic controller gives you a traffic instruction within that deployment, you must follow it.

§ 2 — How Instructions, Signs and Rules Take Precedence

The RVV uses several specific precedence rules. Do not treat them as one universal four-level ladder.

The Legal Precedence Rules

The RVV sets out several precise rules for conflicts:

  • Instructions: Article 84 — valid instructions from authorised persons take precedence over traffic signs and traffic rules.
  • Traffic lights and priority signs: Article 64 — traffic lights take precedence over traffic signs that regulate priority.
  • Traffic signs and general rules: Article 63 — traffic signs take precedence over traffic rules only to the extent that the two are incompatible.
  • Two displayed maximum speeds: Article 63b — if a fixed traffic sign and an electronic signal panel show different maximum speeds, the lower displayed maximum applies.

This is more accurate than saying that every traffic light overrides every road sign in every situation.

Legal Precedence — Key Rules

Apply the specific RVV rule that matches the conflict.

Authorised instruction → over signs & rules
Traffic light → over priority signs
Traffic sign → over incompatible general rule
Two speed signs → lower maximum applies
Authorised Instruction vs Traffic Light Article 84

A valid instruction from an authorised person takes precedence over the traffic light. If you are clearly instructed to proceed while the light is red, follow the instruction. If you are instructed to stop while the light is green, stop.

Only the instruction actually directed at you or your traffic stream takes precedence. A controller merely being present does not make every light or sign irrelevant.
Traffic Light vs Priority Sign Article 64

Traffic lights take precedence over traffic signs that regulate priority. For example, a B1 priority-road sign does not allow you to drive through a red traffic light at a signal-controlled junction.

Do not generalise this into “traffic lights override every road sign.” Maximum-speed conflicts have their own rule: when a fixed sign and an electronic signal panel show different maximum speeds, the lower displayed maximum applies.

Traffic Sign vs General Rule Article 63

A traffic sign takes precedence over a general traffic rule to the extent that the rule is incompatible with the sign. For example, a valid 30 km/h maximum-speed sign applies on a road where the general default would otherwise be 50 km/h.

When Traffic Lights Are Off Check what still applies

If traffic lights are completely off, do not automatically treat the junction as having no regulation at all. First check for priority signs, shark's teeth and other applicable road markings. Where no relevant sign or marking changes the situation, apply the general traffic rules from Chapter 1.

At an otherwise equivalent unregulated junction, the ordinary rule is to give priority to drivers approaching from the right, subject to the statutory exceptions such as trams and paved-versus-unpaved roads.

Worked Scenarios — Applying the Precedence Rules

🟢
Scenario 1: An authorised person clearly signals you to proceed at a red light

What to do: Follow the clear authorised instruction and proceed with appropriate care. Article 84 gives the instruction precedence over the red light.

🔴
Scenario 2: Traffic light is green but controller holds their hand up toward you

What to do: Stop. A clear authorised instruction takes precedence over the green light. Continue only when the instruction allows you to do so.

🟡
Scenario 3: You are on a priority road (B1 sign) but the traffic light shows red

What to do: Stop at the red light. Article 64 provides that traffic lights take precedence over traffic signs that regulate priority, such as B1.

🔵
Scenario 4: No signs, no lights, no controller — you approach an intersection

What to do: Apply the ordinary intersection rules. Give priority to drivers approaching from the right, subject to the statutory exceptions — including the rules for trams and paved versus unpaved roads.

⚫
Scenario 5: Traffic lights are completely off — not functioning

What to do: Check which priority signs and road markings still apply. If none regulate the junction, use the ordinary priority rules. Approach cautiously because other road users may react unpredictably to the failed signals.

🟠
Scenario 6: A matrix sign above your motorway lane shows 90 km/h, but a fixed sign below says 130 km/h

What to do: Drive no faster than 90 km/h. Under Article 63b, if a fixed sign and an electronic signal panel display different maximum speeds, the lower displayed maximum applies. This is a specific speed-sign rule, not an example of a general “traffic light beats road sign” hierarchy.

How to Apply the Rules in Practice

First look for any authorised instruction directed at you. Then identify the traffic lights, signs and road markings that apply. If two sources appear to conflict, use the specific RVV precedence rule for that conflict rather than relying on a universal ranking. If the lights are off, remember that priority signs and road markings may still regulate the junction.

Chapter 3 — What to Take Away

Chapter 3 covers legally binding instructions from authorised persons. The central rule is Article 84: instructions take precedence over traffic signs and traffic rules. Separately, Article 64 says traffic lights take precedence over signs that regulate priority, and Article 63 says traffic signs take precedence over incompatible general traffic rules.

For the exam: recognise the official RVV gesture signals, know that a valid instruction can require you to proceed despite a red light or stop despite a green light, and do not memorise an oversimplified four-level hierarchy. If traffic lights fail, check the remaining signs and road markings before falling back on the general rules.
